title: What Libraries and Frameworks Are
summary: Learn what libraries and frameworks give you, what they cost, and how CSS and JavaScript frameworks differ before you try three of them.
intro: Open almost any job listing for web developers and it names tools: React, Vue, Angular, Bootstrap, Tailwind. Open almost any team's project and its `package.json` lists dozens of packages. None of them can do anything the browser can't, since in the end they all produce HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. What they change is how much you write, how your code is organized, and what you have to learn first. This lesson explains what libraries and frameworks are, the problems they were made to solve, the two very different kinds of CSS framework, how JavaScript frameworks grew from jQuery to React, and what each one costs you. The next three lessons try three of them, and the React course builds on all of it.

steps.title: Libraries versus frameworks
steps.body:
The two words get used loosely, even by the tools themselves, but the difference behind them matters: it decides who's in charge of your code. Knowing which kind you've got tells you how much of your project it will shape, and how hard it would be to take out again.

## A library: you call it

A **library** is code you call when you want it. date-fns from the bundling lesson is one: your code decides when it needs a date in words, calls `formatDistanceToNow`, and gets an answer back. Everything else about your page, how it starts, how it's organized, what happens on a click, is still up to you. You could swap date-fns for another date library by changing the few lines that call it.

Think of a toolbox. You pick up the tool you need, use it, and put it back. The toolbox has no opinion about what you're building.

## A framework: it calls you

A **framework** turns that around. It runs the show, and you fill in the pieces it asks for, in the places and shapes it expects, and it decides when your code runs. That's called **inversion of control**, and it's often summed up as: don't call us, we'll call you.

Think of the frame of a house. It fixes where the walls go, and you choose the doors, the paint, and the furniture. Building inside a frame is much faster than starting from bare ground, and moving a wall later is much harder.

You've already handed over control in a small way. With `addEventListener`, you give the browser a function, and the browser decides when to call it (example 1). A framework does that for your whole page: it decides when each piece of your code runs, what it's given, and what happens to what it returns.

```diagram libraries-and-frameworks-control
Who calls whom: you call a library, and a framework calls you.
```

On the left of the diagram, your code is on top and calls down into a library when it needs to. On the right, the framework is on top, and it calls the pieces of your code.

## Other names you'll meet

- A **toolkit**, or **UI kit**, where UI is short for user interface, the part of an app people see and use, is a library of ready-made pieces for the screen, like buttons, menus, and dialogs. Bootstrap, in the next lesson, is one, with both the CSS and the JavaScript for each piece.
- A **design system** is a company's rules for how its products look and behave, like its colors, its spacing, and how a button acts, plus a kit of components that follows those rules. Google's Material Design, IBM's Carbon, and the UK government's GOV.UK Design System are well-known ones, and many companies build their own.
- A **meta-framework** is a framework built on another one, adding what the first leaves out: pages with their own URLs, loading data, rendering on the server, and building for production. Next.js is built on React, Nuxt on Vue, and SvelteKit on Svelte.

## The lines are blurry

The labels aren't strict. React calls itself a library, since it only handles what's on the screen, yet it calls your code the way a framework does, so most people call it a framework anyway. Tailwind calls itself a CSS framework, though it's really a tool that writes CSS for you. Don't argue about the label. Ask who's in charge. When you call it, you can drop it in and pull it out. When it calls you, it shapes your whole project, and choosing it is a much bigger decision.

examples.title: Who calls whom
examples.prompt: Two statements like the ones in the bundling lesson's notes page. One calls a library. The other hands the browser a function to call later.
examples.explanation: In the first statement, your code is in charge: it calls `formatDistanceToNow` at the moment it chooses, waits for the answer, and carries on with it. That's how you use a library. In the second, you pass a function to `addEventListener`, and nothing happens yet. The browser keeps the function and calls it later, once for each click, or never. You wrote that function, but you don't decide when it runs. That's inversion of control, in one line. A framework works the same way on a bigger scale: you write a function for each piece of the page, and the framework calls them when the page starts, when the data changes, and when someone moves to another page.

steps.title: The problems they solve
steps.body:
Every popular library or framework exists because something was painful without it. Knowing what the pain was tells you when a tool earns its place, and when the browser has since fixed the problem and the tool is only adding weight.

## Browsers that disagreed

In the 2000s, browsers did the same things in different ways. Internet Explorer, the browser most people used, added event listeners with `attachEvent` while the others used `addEventListener`, and fetching data without a reload took different code in each. Even finding elements was hard: most browsers didn't have `querySelectorAll` until 2009, so finding everything with a class meant walking the page yourself. Every site carried its own fixes for each browser, and each new browser version broke a few of them.

Libraries like jQuery hid all that behind one set of functions that worked everywhere, which is a big part of why the jQuery lesson exists. Today, browsers follow shared standards and update themselves every few weeks, and Baseline, from the rendering lesson, tells you what works everywhere. This problem is mostly solved, by the browsers themselves.

## Many hands, one project

Ten developers writing buttons by hand make ten slightly different buttons. Ten developers organizing code their own way make a project nobody can find their way around. A framework gives a team one way to do the common things: where files go, how a page splits into pieces, how those pieces get their data. A new hire who knows the framework already knows half the project on their first day, and that matters as much as speed.

## Parts nobody should build twice

Some parts of a page look simple and aren't. A dropdown menu has to open on a click, close on a click anywhere else or on Escape, move with the arrow keys, stay on screen near the edge of the window, and tell a screen reader whether it's open. A date picker, a sortable table, or a search box that suggests answers is worse. Toolkits hand you these parts finished, and tested in more browsers than you own.

## Keeping the page in sync with the data

This is the big one. Recall the end of the JavaScript lessons: you keep your data in variables, and the page shows it. Every change to the data means changing every spot on the page that shows it. With a cart count in the header, a list of items, a total, and a checkout button that turns off when the cart is empty, one click means four updates. Forget one, and the page shows something that isn't true, as example 1 does. As an app grows, the updates multiply, and the bugs with them.

Modern JavaScript frameworks attack this head on. Instead of writing each change to the page, you describe what the page should look like for any data, and the framework works out what to change whenever the data changes. That's what the React course is about, and part 4 shows the idea.

## Accessibility done once

Getting every detail right for keyboard users and screen readers takes care, and one is easy to miss. A modal dialog, the kind of box that covers the page until you deal with it, has to move focus into itself when it opens, keep Tab from wandering to the page behind it, close on Escape, hide the rest of the page from screen readers, and put focus back on the button that opened it. A good library gets that right once, for everyone who uses it. The HTML lessons showed that the browser's own `<dialog>` element now does most of this, which is the first problem's story again: the platform catches up, and the library becomes optional.

examples.title: Four updates for one click
examples.prompt: A cart kept in sync with the page by hand. The helper functions `itemRow`, `total`, and `formatPrice` build a row, add up the prices, and format a price.
examples.explanation: Adding an item updates four spots on the page by hand. Removing one updates only three: the line that turns the checkout button off when the cart is empty was forgotten. Empty the cart, and the button still offers to check out. No error appears anywhere. The page just shows something false. None of this code is hard, and that's the problem: every new feature that shows the cart, like a badge on a menu or a free-delivery note, needs a new line in every function that changes the cart, and each forgotten line is a bug like this one. The JavaScript lessons fixed it with one render function that rebuilds the page from the data. Frameworks take that idea and make it fast and tidy, so you never write the updates at all.

steps.title: CSS frameworks: components or utilities
steps.body:
CSS frameworks come in two very different styles, and a page written in one looks nothing like a page written in the other. You'll meet both at work, and the next lessons teach one of each, so it's worth seeing first what each does to your HTML and to your CSS.

## Component classes

A **component class** names a whole piece of the page. Bootstrap writes a blue button as `class="btn btn-primary"` (example 1). `btn` brings the padding, the rounded corners, and the looks for hover and focus, and `btn-primary` brings the colors. The rules live in Bootstrap's stylesheet, and you never see them unless you go looking.

- **What it's good at:** short, readable HTML, a consistent look on the first day, and a team that agrees on what a button is.
- **What it costs:** every site that uses it looks alike unless you change it, and changing it means overriding Bootstrap's rules with your own, which brings back the specificity fights from the cascade lesson. You also send the whole stylesheet, 232 kB, or 31 kB compressed, unless you build a smaller one.

## Utility classes

A **utility class** does one small job, like setting the padding or a color, and you build each piece out of many of them, right in the HTML. Tailwind writes the same button as `class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 font-semibold text-white"`, plus a few more classes for hover and focus (example 2). Each class stands for one or two CSS declarations, and the stylesheet holds only the classes your pages use.

- **What it's good at:** you never invent class names or switch between files, the stylesheet stays small because it's built from what you use, and deleting the HTML deletes its styles with it. A fixed scale of sizes and colors keeps everything consistent.
- **What it costs:** long class lists that take getting used to, a new set of names to learn, and the same list repeated wherever a button appears, unless you wrap it in a component of your own.

## Plain CSS with tokens

The third choice is no framework: your own class names, like `.button`, with your own rules, built on **design tokens**, custom properties from the CSS lessons that hold the site's colors, sizes, and spacing in one place (example 3). CSS now has nesting, layers, `:has()`, and container queries, so this is far easier than it was when frameworks took over.

- **What it's good at:** no dependency, nothing to learn but CSS, and full control.
- **What it costs:** you design, build, and document every piece yourself, and on a big team, keeping everyone's CSS consistent is your job.

## Side by side

```diagram libraries-and-frameworks-three-buttons
One button, three ways. What changes is where its styles live.
```

| | Component classes | Utility classes | Plain CSS with tokens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The HTML | short, like `btn btn-primary` | long, a class per property | short, with your own names |
| Where the styles are | the framework's stylesheet | in the HTML | your stylesheet |
| Stylesheet size | the whole framework, unless trimmed | only what's used | what you write |
| Changing the look | override its rules or variables | change the classes | change your rules |
| Example | Bootstrap | Tailwind | your own CSS |

None of them is right for everything. Bootstrap fits a team that wants a finished look fast, Tailwind fits a team building its own look out of components, and plain CSS fits small sites and teams that want no dependencies at all.

examples.title: Component classes, the Bootstrap way
examples.prompt: Bootstrap's stylesheet, linked from a CDN, and one button that uses it.
examples.explanation: Two classes, and the button is done: padding, rounded corners, a blue background, white text, and its own looks for hover, focus, and disabled. All of it lives in Bootstrap's stylesheet, loaded from a CDN on the first line, and part 5 explains its `integrity` attribute. Swap `btn-primary` for `btn-outline-danger` and it becomes a red outlined button. That's the appeal: you pick from a menu. To make a button Bootstrap doesn't have, you write CSS of your own that changes parts of Bootstrap's, and the Bootstrap lesson shows the tidy way to do that.

examples.title: Utility classes, the Tailwind way
examples.prompt: The same button in Tailwind. Tailwind reads this HTML and writes a stylesheet with only these rules in it.
examples.code:
<button type="button" class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 font-semibold text-white hover:bg-blue-700 focus-visible:outline-2 focus-visible:outline-offset-2 focus-visible:outline-blue-600">
  Save
</button>
examples.explanation: Each class is one decision. `rounded-lg` rounds the corners, `bg-blue-600` picks a blue from Tailwind's color scale, `px-4` and `py-2` set the padding on the left and right and on the top and bottom, and `font-semibold` and `text-white` style the text. The prefixes are conditions: `hover:` applies its class only while the pointer is over the button, and `focus-visible:` only when it has keyboard focus. Tailwind finds these names in your files and writes just their rules. For a page with only this button, the whole stylesheet, Tailwind's reset included, came to about 6 kB, and under 2 kB compressed. The Tailwind lesson covers every piece.

examples.title: Plain CSS with tokens
examples.prompt: The same button with no framework: tokens at the top of your stylesheet, and one class of your own. The HTML is `<button type="button" class="button">Save</button>`.
examples.explanation: The tokens at the top hold the decisions: an accent color and a darker shade of it for hover, one corner radius, and two spacing steps. `.button` uses them through `var()`, and its hover and focus rules are nested inside it with `&`, both from the CSS lessons. Change `--color-accent` and every button, link, and border that uses it changes with it. Both frameworks are built on this same idea: Bootstrap's components read variables that start with `--bs-`, and Tailwind's colors and sizes are custom properties too. The difference is that here, you write and own every rule.

steps.title: JavaScript frameworks at a glance
steps.body:
The code you'll maintain at work comes from every era of the web, and each era's code looks different, so knowing the eras lets you recognize what you're looking at. The story also explains why React works the way it does, which gives you a head start on the React course.

```diagram libraries-and-frameworks-timeline
Twenty years of JavaScript tools, and the problem each one took on.
```

## 2006: jQuery

**jQuery** made one promise: write less, do more, in every browser. You picked elements with CSS selectors, like `$(".menu li")`, and changed them with short methods you could chain one after another. It smoothed over every browser difference of its day and made fetching data without a reload easy. It became so common that browsers copied its best ideas: `querySelectorAll`, `classList`, and `fetch` all came after it. It still runs on a huge share of the web, and the jQuery lesson teaches you to read it.

jQuery made changing the page easy, but it didn't help you organize an app. Big jQuery code turned into what developers called spaghetti: handlers everywhere, each changing the page directly, and nobody sure which one changed what.

## 2010: Backbone and AngularJS

The next wave added structure. **Backbone.js** split code into **models**, which hold the data, and **views**, which draw it, and a view redrew itself when its model announced a change. **AngularJS**, from Google, went further with **two-way data binding**: change a value in your code and the page changed, and type into a field and the value in your code changed. To notice changes, AngularJS rechecked every value it watched after anything happened, which got slow on big pages. **Angular**, a full rewrite in 2016, replaced it, and old AngularJS apps still need porting.

## 2013: React

**React**, from Facebook, changed the question. Instead of writing how to change the page, you write what the page should look like for the current data, as a function, and React works out the changes itself. That style is called **declarative**: you declare the result. The older style, giving the steps one at a time, is **imperative**. Examples 1 and 2 show the same list both ways.

React also made **components** the building block of everything. A component is a function that returns one piece of the page, like a note list or a button, and it can be built from other components. Data flows one way, down from a component to the ones inside it, so it's easy to see where any value came from. When the data changes, React calls your component again, compares the new result with the last one, and changes only the parts of the page that differ.

## After React

The ideas spread, each with its own trade-offs. **Vue** (2014) uses templates that look like HTML and tracks which data each part of the page reads. **Svelte** (2016) is a **compiler**: it turns your components into plain JavaScript at build time, so less framework code goes to the browser. **Solid**, which reached version 1.0 in 2021, looks like React but updates only the exact spots that changed, using **signals**, values that know who reads them. Angular, Vue, and Svelte have taken up signals since. Lighter tools, like htmx and Alpine.js, add behavior to HTML with attributes, for pages that need a little interactivity rather than a whole app.

The browser has its own way to make components, too: **Web Components** let you define new HTML elements, like `<note-list>`, that work in any page and next to any framework.

## Meta-frameworks

React draws the page and nothing more. It leaves out pages with their own URLs, loading data, rendering on the server, and building for production. Meta-frameworks bundle those choices together: **Next.js** (2016) on React, **Nuxt** on Vue, **SvelteKit** on Svelte, and **Astro**, which sends plain HTML and adds JavaScript only to the pieces that need it. Hack University's Next.js course comes right after the React course.

examples.title: Imperative: every step by hand
examples.prompt: Adding a note to a list the way the JavaScript lessons did. `notes` is an array, `list` is the `<ul>`, and `count` is a paragraph above it.
examples.explanation: Every line is a step: change the data, make an element, fill it in, put it on the page, then fix the count. It's clear, and it works, and it's exactly what jQuery-era code did with shorter method names. The trouble is what it leaves to you. Removing a note needs its own steps, and so does editing one, and each must remember the count. If notes can also be sorted or filtered, every one of those functions has to keep the list in the right order. The page is only right if every function that touches the data remembers every spot that shows it.

examples.title: Declarative: describe the result
examples.prompt: The same piece of the page as a React component. The React course teaches this from the start, so read it for the idea, not every symbol.
examples.explanation: The parts that look like HTML are **JSX**: HTML written inside JavaScript, which the build step from the bundling lesson turns into plain function calls. Curly braces drop a JavaScript value in, so `{notes.length}` shows the count, and `notes.map` turns each note into a list item. Now notice what's missing: nothing finds an element, appends an item, or updates the count. The function describes the whole piece for whatever notes it's given. When a note is added, React calls `NoteList` again with the new array, compares the result with what's on the screen, and adds one list item and changes the count by itself. The count can't be forgotten, because nothing updates it by hand.

steps.title: Costs, and how to add one
steps.body:
Every library or framework you add saves you work and costs you something, and the costs are easy to miss because they show up later. A strong developer weighs both before adding one, and knows how to add it cleanly once the answer is yes.

## What it costs

- **Bytes.** Visitors download it, and their phones have to parse and run it before the page responds. In our builds, React and React DOM came to 219 kB, or 69 kB compressed, for a page that only says Hello. Bootstrap's CSS is 31 kB compressed and its JavaScript 24 kB, and jQuery is 28 kB.
- **Learning.** Everyone on the team has to learn it, and everyone you hire after them.
- **Lock-in.** A framework shapes your whole project, so leaving it means a rewrite. That's why a framework choice often outlives the people who made it.
- **Upgrades.** New major versions break things on purpose. AngularJS to Angular was a rewrite, Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery, and jQuery 4 removed more than a dozen old functions. Someone has to do that work, or the project stays on an old version that stops getting security fixes.
- **Its future.** When nobody maintains a project anymore, the fixes stop, and you're left holding it.

## Use the platform first

Much of what libraries did is now built into the browser. `querySelectorAll` and `classList` do what jQuery's selecting did, `fetch` replaces its functions for fetching data, `<dialog>` and the `popover` attribute give you dialogs and menus, Grid and Flexbox replace grid frameworks, custom properties give you themes, and `Intl.DateTimeFormat` formats dates in any language. Before you install anything, check whether the browser already does it. Every package you don't add is one you never have to update.

## Two ways to add one

The quick way is a `<link>` or `<script>` tag that loads the library from a **CDN**, the servers around the world from the caching lesson. There's no install and no build step, which suits a demo, a prototype, or a site with no build at all. Pin an exact version in the URL, and add an `integrity` attribute.

That attribute is **Subresource Integrity**, or SRI: a hash of the file you expect, worked out with a hash function like SHA-384. The browser hashes the file it downloads, and if the two don't match, because the CDN was broken into or the file was changed, it refuses to use it. `crossorigin="anonymous"` goes with it, since the browser can only check a file from another origin when it's fetched in CORS mode, the way the caching lesson showed fonts are. Example 1 shows where the hash comes from.

The way teams do it is npm and a bundler: `npm install` the package and `import` it in your code, the way the bundling lesson added date-fns (example 2). The lockfile pins the exact version, the bundler takes only what you use and gives it a hashed name, and the file comes from your own origin, with no extra connection and no third party to trust.

## Questions to ask first

1. Does the browser already do this?
2. How big is it, really? Build with it and read the sizes Vite prints.
3. Is it maintained? Look at when it last had a release, and whether questions about it get answered.
4. How many people use it? A popular package has had its bugs found by others first, and answers to your questions are already online.
5. Is it accessible, and does it work with the rest of your project?
6. What's its license? Most are free to use, but check before you ship.
7. How hard would it be to remove later?

A library you can pull out in an afternoon is a small bet. A framework is a big one, and it's worth a day of reading and a small trial project before you commit.

examples.title: Where an integrity hash comes from
examples.prompt: On a Mac or Linux, download Bootstrap's stylesheet from the CDN and work out its SHA-384 hash.
examples.explanation: curl downloads the file and passes it along to `openssl`, a tool for encryption and hashing that comes with macOS and Linux. `dgst -sha384 -binary` works out the file's SHA-384 hash, and `base64 -A` writes it out as text. Put `sha384-` in front and it's the value for the `integrity` attribute, exactly the one in part 3's example and in Bootstrap's own docs. Change a single byte of the file and the hash comes out completely different, which is the point: the browser checks the file against it every time. Most libraries print the tag in their docs with the hash already filled in, so you'll rarely run this yourself, but now you know what that long string is.

examples.title: The same library, from npm
examples.prompt: After `npm install bootstrap`, these lines in `src/main.js` replace the CDN tags. The page has a dialog with the id `confirm` and a button with the id `delete`.
examples.explanation: The first import pulls in Bootstrap's stylesheet, which Vite turns into a hashed CSS file, like the notes page's. The second imports only the code for Bootstrap's modal dialog, from its own file inside the package. In our build that came to 23 kB, where importing all of Bootstrap's JavaScript came to 81 kB. The rest is the DOM code you know: make the dialog object, and show it on a click. The version comes from `package-lock.json`, so every computer that builds the site gets the same one, and your visitors download it from your own origin. The next lesson is all about Bootstrap.

recap:
- You call a library when you want it, and a framework calls your code: that's inversion of control.
- Toolkits give you ready-made parts, design systems add rules for using them, and meta-frameworks build on frameworks.
- Frameworks were made to fix browser differences, team consistency, hard parts, accessibility, and keeping the page in sync with data.
- Component classes like Bootstrap's name whole pieces, utility classes like Tailwind's do one job each, and plain CSS uses your own tokens.
- JavaScript tools went from jQuery's imperative steps to React's declarative components, then compilers and signals.
- Every dependency costs bytes, learning, lock-in, and upgrades, so check what the browser already does first.
- A CDN tag needs a pinned version and an integrity hash, and teams usually install with npm and bundle instead.
